These include residential refrigeration, as well as residential and commercial lighting and electronics. 3 Dynamic Pricing Studies: In 2021, CPUC began investing in a line of research studies to explore the impacts of such pricing programs. The first of these studies (Gerke et al. 2022) developed a hypothetical multi-component dynamic tariff for 2019, conceptually similar to the CalFUSE tariff, and considered the impacts on annual customer bills and month-to-month bill variability, compared to that year’s prevailing tariffs, under a worst-case scenario in which customers do not alter their energy consumption patterns. This was the tariff that was also leveraged in the analysis for the Phase 4 report. Additionally, various designs for 2-part “subscription” tariffs were explored in this study. The report originally focused on “universal” tariffs where all customers in a given IOU territory are exposed to the same dynamic price. An addendum to the report later explored an alternate set of prices that were specific to each customer class, such that the tariff would be revenue neutral to each class’s average load shape. A second dynamic pricing study (Smith et al., 2024, pending) then explored the electricity demand and bill impacts if customers were to respond to dynamic prices based on an assumed level of price elasticity. The same class-adjusted tariffs from the prior report’s addendum were used, and again the study focused solely on 2019 due to the availability of customer-level AMI data for that year. A range of elasticity scenarios were explored in this “Elastic Impacts Study”, but data on customer elasticity to electricity prices is limited to real-time pricing programs that existed before our current era of internet-connected devices, steep duck curves on the system level (causing more dramatic differences in prices), and electrified end uses such as EVs. Therefore, the Elastic Impacts Study was limited in its ability to estimate price responsive capabilities at the end-use level and capture the more dramatic load response thought to be possible from highly connected, highly flexible loads. The current California Price Response Potential Study builds on the Phase 4 Report and Elastic Impacts Study by continuing to focus on understanding the potential impacts of dynamic pricing on customer bills, system load, and the cost-effectiveness of automation technologies.
